objectives: Distinguish stenosis from regurgitation and localize valvular murmurs by timing and auscultation site.
Explain how echocardiography and Doppler quantify valve lesions, including the Bernoulli pressure gradient.
Summarize aortic stenosis with TAVR, mitral disease, and common congenital defects.

slides.title: Stenosis, regurgitation, and the art of auscultation
slides.body:
A heart valve can fail in two opposite ways. **Stenosis** is a valve that will not open fully, obstructing forward flow and forcing the upstream chamber to generate higher pressure. **Regurgitation (insufficiency)** is a valve that will not close fully, allowing backward leakage and volume-overloading the chambers. A valve may suffer both (mixed disease). Each of the four valves can be stenotic or regurgitant, giving a matrix of lesions whose physical signs follow directly from the cardiac cycle.

**Auscultation** with the stethoscope — refined since **Rene Laennec** invented the instrument in 1816 — localizes murmurs by where they are loudest and when in the cycle they occur. The four classic listening posts: **aortic area** (right second intercostal space), **pulmonic area** (left second intercostal space), **tricuspid area** (left lower sternal border), and **mitral area** (cardiac apex). Timing relative to the heart sounds **S1** (mitral/tricuspid closure) and **S2** (aortic/pulmonic closure) is decisive:

- **Systolic murmurs** (between S1 and S2) include **aortic stenosis** (a harsh crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur radiating to the carotids) and **mitral regurgitation** (a blowing holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla).
- **Diastolic murmurs** (between S2 and S1) include **aortic regurgitation** (an early decrescendo blow heard at the left sternal border) and **mitral stenosis** (a low-pitched rumble with an opening snap, heard at the apex).

The logic is simple once anchored to the cycle: a stenotic **semilunar** valve (aortic, pulmonic) obstructs **ejection**, so its murmur is **systolic**; a stenotic **AV** valve (mitral, tricuspid) obstructs **filling**, so its murmur is **diastolic**. Regurgitation reverses this — a leaking semilunar valve floods back during **diastole**, while a leaking AV valve leaks during **systole**.

Bedside maneuvers sharpen the diagnosis: **handgrip** increases afterload and accentuates mitral and aortic regurgitation; **Valsalva** decreases preload and softens most murmurs except **hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy** and **mitral valve prolapse**, which paradoxically intensify. Associated signs add information: a **wide pulse pressure** and bounding 'water-hammer' pulse suggest aortic regurgitation; a **slow-rising, low-volume (pulsus parvus et tardus)** carotid pulse suggests severe aortic stenosis. Historically, **rheumatic fever** following streptococcal infection was the dominant cause of valve disease worldwide (especially mitral stenosis); in high-income countries, **degenerative calcific** disease of aging and congenital abnormalities now predominate. The trained ear, combined with the cardiac-cycle framework, lets the cardiologist form a precise hypothesis before any imaging — a hypothesis that **echocardiography** then confirms and quantifies.

slides.title: Echocardiography and Doppler quantification
slides.body:
**Echocardiography** — cardiac ultrasound — is the workhorse of structural cardiology, building on the **Doppler effect** described by **Christian Doppler** in 1842 and the medical ultrasound pioneered by **Inge Edler** and **Carl Hellmuth Hertz** in Sweden in the 1950s. A piezoelectric transducer emits high-frequency sound (2-10 MHz) and times the echoes to construct images and measure velocities.

Several modes serve different purposes:

- **2D echocardiography** shows real-time anatomy: chamber sizes, wall thickness and motion, valve structure, and **ejection fraction** by tracing volumes.
- **M-mode** plots a single scan line over time, giving precise timing and dimensions.
- **Doppler** measures **blood velocity** by the frequency shift of reflected ultrasound. **Color Doppler** overlays velocity as color to visualize regurgitant jets and shunts; **continuous-wave and pulsed-wave Doppler** quantify peak velocities.
- **Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)** places the probe in the esophagus, just behind the left atrium, for superb resolution of the mitral valve, left atrial appendage, and prosthetic valves.

The quantitative heart of Doppler echo is the **simplified Bernoulli equation**, which converts a measured velocity into a **pressure gradient** across a narrowed valve:

$$\Delta P \approx 4 v^2$$

where $\Delta P$ is the pressure gradient in mmHg and $v$ is the peak jet velocity in m/s. For example, an aortic jet of $v = 4$ m/s implies $\Delta P \approx 4 \times 16 = 64$ mmHg — a severe gradient. This formula is a clinical simplification of the full **Bernoulli principle** (named for **Daniel Bernoulli**, 1738), which relates the energy of flowing fluid; the convective acceleration term $4v^2$ dominates across a discrete stenosis, and the factor 4 absorbs the blood density and unit conversions.

Valve area is estimated by the **continuity equation**, an expression of conservation of mass: flow is preserved across regions, so $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$, allowing the stenotic **aortic valve area** to be computed from the velocity-time integrals proximal to and across the valve. A normal aortic valve area is ~3-4 cm$^2$; **severe aortic stenosis** is defined as an area below 1.0 cm$^2$, a mean gradient above 40 mmHg, or a peak jet velocity above 4 m/s. Regurgitation severity is graded from jet width, regurgitant volume, and the **vena contracta** (the narrowest neck of the jet). Beyond valves, echo detects **pericardial effusion** and **tamponade**, intracardiac thrombus, vegetations of **endocarditis**, and congenital shunts. Because it is noninvasive, portable, radiation-free, and quantitative, echocardiography has become the indispensable extension of the stethoscope, turning the qualitative murmur into hard numbers that drive decisions about timing of surgery or intervention.

slides.title: Aortic stenosis, mitral disease, and congenital defects
slides.body:
**Aortic stenosis (AS)** is the most common valve lesion requiring intervention in the developed world, usually from age-related **calcific degeneration** of a trileaflet valve or from a congenitally **bicuspid aortic valve** (present in ~1-2% of people and prone to early calcification). As the valve narrows, the left ventricle faces enormous **afterload**, hypertrophies concentrically (raising wall stress per the law of Laplace), and eventually fails. The classic triad of symptomatic severe AS is **angina, syncope, and heart failure (dyspnea)** — the onset of symptoms marks a sharp drop in survival, the trigger for valve replacement. For decades the only option was **surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR)** with a mechanical or bioprosthetic valve. The transformative advance was **transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)**, first performed in a human by **Alain Cribier** in 2002: a collapsible prosthetic valve is delivered by catheter (usually transfemoral) and deployed within the diseased valve, without open-heart surgery. Landmark trials (**PARTNER** for the balloon-expandable Edwards Sapien and **CoreValve/Evolut** for the self-expanding device) extended TAVR from inoperable patients to high-, intermediate-, and now low-surgical-risk patients, making it the default for many older adults.

**Mitral valve disease** takes two main forms. **Mitral regurgitation (MR)** — leakage during systole — may be **primary** (degenerative, from **mitral valve prolapse**, the **Barlow** or fibroelastic deficiency, or ruptured chordae) or **secondary/functional** (the leaflets are normal but a dilated or ischemic ventricle tethers them open). Severe MR volume-overloads the left atrium and ventricle. Treatment ranges from **surgical mitral repair** (preferred over replacement when feasible) to **transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER)** with the **MitraClip**, which clips the leaflets together to reduce the leak. **Mitral stenosis (MS)** is now most often **rheumatic**, fusing the commissures; it can be relieved by **percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty** or surgery and predisposes to **atrial fibrillation** and left-atrial thrombus.

**Congenital heart defects**, present in ~1% of births, are the structural lesions one is born with. The most common acyanotic shunts move blood left-to-right: the **ventricular septal defect (VSD)**, the **atrial septal defect (ASD)**, and the **patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)** — a persistent fetal connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery that normally closes after birth (relevant to the work of **Helen Taussig** and **Robert Gross**, who ligated the first PDA in 1938). **Coarctation of the aorta** is a narrowing of the aortic arch causing upper-body hypertension. Cyanotic lesions, mixing deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, include **tetralogy of Fallot** — described by **Etienne-Louis Fallot** and surgically palliated by the **Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt** (Alfred Blalock, Helen Taussig, and Vivien Thomas, 1944), a landmark in pediatric cardiac surgery — and **transposition of the great arteries**. A large uncorrected left-to-right shunt can eventually reverse into a right-to-left shunt as pulmonary pressures rise, the irreversible **Eisenmenger syndrome**. Recognizing these structural lesions, quantifying them by echo, and timing their repair is the domain of structural and congenital cardiology.

question.question: A harsh crescendo-decrescendo SYSTOLIC murmur heard best at the right second intercostal space and radiating to the carotids is most characteristic of:
question.explanation: Aortic stenosis produces a harsh systolic ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur at the aortic area (right second intercostal space) that radiates to the carotids. Mitral stenosis is a diastolic rumble at the apex; aortic regurgitation is a diastolic decrescendo blow; mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.

hints: A stenotic semilunar valve obstructs ejection, so the murmur is systolic.
Radiation to the carotids points to the aortic valve.
slides.workedSolution: Aortic stenosis: systolic crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur at the aortic area, radiating to the carotids, often with a slow-rising (parvus et tardus) pulse. The semilunar valve obstructs ejection, hence the systolic timing.

question.question: Doppler echocardiography measures a peak aortic jet velocity of 5 m/s. Using the simplified Bernoulli equation, peak gradient = 4 * v^2, compute the peak pressure gradient in mmHg.
question.hint: Square the velocity (5^2 = 25), then multiply by 4.

question.question: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), first performed in a human by Alain Cribier in 2002, treats which condition?
options: Mitral regurgitation from a flail leaflet
Severe aortic stenosis, by deploying a prosthetic valve via catheter
Atrial septal defect, by device closure
question.explanation: TAVR delivers a collapsible prosthetic valve by catheter to treat severe aortic stenosis without open-heart surgery; trials (PARTNER, CoreValve/Evolut) extended it across surgical-risk categories. MR is treated by surgical repair or MitraClip (TEER); ASD by device closure; heart block by a pacemaker.

hints: TAVR is named for the aortic valve.
It addresses a valve that will not open (stenosis), not a leak or a shunt.
slides.workedSolution: TAVR (Cribier, 2002) replaces a stenotic aortic valve via catheter, now standard for many patients across the risk spectrum. The MitraClip/TEER addresses mitral regurgitation, a different lesion.

question.question: An elderly man with exertional syncope and a systolic murmur
question.prompt: An 80-year-old reports increasing breathlessness on exertion and recently fainted while climbing stairs. On exam he has a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids and a slow-rising carotid pulse. Echocardiography shows a heavily calcified aortic valve with a peak jet velocity of 4.5 m/s and a valve area of 0.8 cm squared. Using the Bernoulli relation and the criteria for severe aortic stenosis, explain why this is severe symptomatic disease, why the onset of symptoms (the angina-syncope-dyspnea triad) is so ominous, and what definitive treatment options exist for an 80-year-old, comparing surgical replacement with the transcatheter approach.

question.question: Which of the following is a CYANOTIC congenital heart defect, classically palliated by the Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt?
question.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic lesion (right-to-left shunt) classically palliated by the Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt (Blalock, Taussig, and Vivien Thomas, 1944). ASD, VSD, and PDA are acyanotic left-to-right shunts (though a large shunt can later reverse into Eisenmenger physiology).

hints: Cyanotic means deoxygenated blood reaches the systemic circulation (right-to-left).
The historic shunt by Blalock, Taussig, and Thomas treated this four-part defect.
slides.workedSolution: Tetralogy of Fallot is the classic cyanotic defect palliated by the Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt (1944). ASD/VSD/PDA are acyanotic left-to-right shunts unless they reverse into Eisenmenger syndrome.
